profile.feeling: Warmth: ginger tea for a cold, the aromatic base of almost every stir-fry.

senses.def: Jiang, a common surname (姜 was a surname before simplification merged it with 薑 ‘ginger’)

examples.text: 感冒了就喝一碗姜汤。
examples.tr: When you catch a cold, drink a bowl of ginger tea.
examples.py: Gǎnmào le jiù hē yì wǎn jiāngtāng.

examples.text: 炒菜的时候放一点儿姜。
examples.tr: Put in a little ginger when you stir-fry.
examples.py: Chǎo cài de shíhou fàng yìdiǎnr jiāng.

examples.text: 我买一块姜。
examples.tr: I’ll buy a piece of ginger.
examples.py: Wǒ mǎi yí kuài jiāng.

collocations.tr: spring onion, ginger and garlic — the aromatic trio

phrases.tr: ginger is hotter when it’s old
phrases.meaning: experience wins; the old hands know best

phrases.tr: eat radish in winter and ginger in summer
phrases.meaning: folk health advice about eating with the seasons

synonyms.nuance: ‘raw ginger’: the fresh root; on labels and in recipes, and the everyday word in many Mandarin dialects (Xi’an, Chengdu, Nanjing …)

etymology.text: Traditional 薑 was originally written 䕬, a phono-semantic compound: 艸 ‘plant’ + phonetic 彊. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *kjaŋ ‘ginger’; compare Burmese ချင်း (hkyang:). The simplified form 姜 was originally a different character, the surname Jiang.

funFacts: Simplification merged two characters: 薑 ‘ginger’ and the surname 姜 are both 姜 on the Mainland, but stay distinct in Taiwan and Hong Kong.
English ginger, German Ingwer, Arabic زَنْجَبِيل (zanjabīl) and Turkish zencefil all go back to one Indic word; Chinese 姜 is unrelated — an inherited Sino-Tibetan word.
pitfalls: 姜 has 女 at the bottom; 美 (měi, ‘beautiful’) has 大 — easy to mix up.
In traditional characters ginger is 薑; writing 姜 for ginger there reads as the surname.
subtleties: 嫩姜 (young ginger) is mild and often pickled; 老姜 (old ginger) is fibrous and hot — which is what the saying 姜还是老的辣 plays on.

profile.feeling: Northern dumplings with a bright anise smell; a spice-shop word too.

senses.def: fennel; in China above all its feathery leaves (茴香苗), eaten as a vegetable; the bulb is 球茎茴香
short for 八角茴香, star anise (the spice)

examples.text: 北方人爱吃茴香馅儿的饺子。
examples.tr: Northerners love dumplings with a fennel filling.
examples.py: Běifāngrén ài chī huíxiāng xiànr de jiǎozi.

examples.text: 超市里也有球茎茴香，可以做沙拉。
examples.tr: The supermarket also has bulb fennel; you can make a salad with it.
examples.py: Chāoshì li yě yǒu qiújīng huíxiāng, kěyǐ zuò shālā.

examples.text: 我买一把茴香。
examples.tr: I’ll buy a bunch of fennel greens.
examples.py: Wǒ mǎi yì bǎ huíxiāng.

phrases.text: 茴香豆的茴字，怎样写的？
phrases.tr: how do you write the 茴 of 茴香豆?
phrases.meaning: Kong Yiji’s pedantic question; quoted for useless, show-off erudition

synonyms.nuance: explicitly the bulb (Florence fennel), the vegetable in the picture; plain 茴香 suggests the leafy greens

etymology.text: 茴 (grass radical 艸 + phonetic 回) + 香 (‘fragrant’): the fragrant plant huí.

funFacts: In Lu Xun’s story 孔乙己 the scholar Kong Yiji eats 茴香豆 — broad beans cooked with 茴香 spice — and boasts that the 回 of 茴 can be written four ways.
Greek μάραθο is fennel — and the town of Marathon is named after the fennel that grew there.
pitfalls: In recipes 茴香 alone can mean star anise (short for 八角茴香) — check whether it is a spice or a vegetable.
In Chinese markets 茴香 is usually the leafy greens; ask for 球茎茴香 if you want the bulb.
subtleties: 小茴香 is fennel seed; 大茴香 or 八角 is star anise, a different plant with a similar smell.

profile.feeling: Tropical south (Guangxi, Hainan), starch factories, bubble-tea pearls.

examples.text: 木薯粉可以做珍珠奶茶里的珍珠。
examples.tr: Cassava (tapioca) starch is used to make the pearls in bubble tea.
examples.py: Mùshǔ fěn kěyǐ zuò zhēnzhū nǎichá li de zhēnzhū.

examples.text: 木薯不能生吃，要煮熟。
examples.tr: Cassava can’t be eaten raw; it has to be cooked through.
examples.py: Mùshǔ bù néng shēng chī, yào zhǔshú.

examples.text: 广西种了很多木薯。
examples.tr: A lot of cassava is grown in Guangxi.
examples.py: Guǎngxī zhòng le hěn duō mùshǔ.

synonyms.nuance: ‘tree tuber’ — the usual word in Taiwan and in Hakka and Min dialects

etymology.text: 木 (‘tree, wood’) + 薯 (‘tuber, yam’): the ‘tree tuber’ — the plant is a woody shrub.

funFacts: The chewy ‘pearls’ (珍珠) in bubble tea are made from cassava starch.
Taiwanese 树薯 ‘tree tuber’ and Mainland 木薯 ‘wood tuber’ describe the plant the same way.
pitfalls: Raw cassava contains toxic compounds that release cyanide — it must be peeled and cooked thoroughly.
Don’t confuse 木薯 (cassava) with 红薯 (sweet potato) or 山药 (Chinese yam).
subtleties: 薯 is the shared ‘tuber’ character: 红薯, 马铃薯, 木薯 — the first character tells you which one.

profile.feeling: A spring delicacy, a little upmarket; Germany’s white Spargel.

senses.def: reed shoot (the young shoot of the common reed)

examples.text: 芦笋炒虾仁很清淡。
examples.tr: Asparagus stir-fried with shrimp is light and delicate.
examples.py: Lúsǔn chǎo xiārén hěn qīngdàn.

examples.text: 春天的芦笋最嫩。
examples.tr: Asparagus is most tender in spring.
examples.py: Chūntiān de lúsǔn zuì nèn.

examples.text: 德国人很喜欢吃白芦笋。
examples.tr: Germans love white asparagus.
examples.py: Déguórén hěn xǐhuan chī bái lúsǔn.

synonyms.nuance: the botanical name (Asparagus officinalis); not used when shopping
the Cantonese word

etymology.text: 芦 (‘reed’) + 笋 (‘shoot’): literally ‘reed shoot’, the word’s first meaning in Wiktionary; asparagus spears look like reed shoots.

funFacts: English asparagus, German Spargel, Greek σπαράγγι and Russian спаржа all come from Greek ἀσπάραγος.
White asparagus is the same plant as green, grown under mounds of soil so it never sees light.
pitfalls: 笋 on its own is the bamboo shoot (竹笋); 芦笋 is a completely different plant.
Traditional 蘆筍 has 旬 under the bamboo radical; simplified 笋 has 尹.
subtleties: German Spargelzeit (asparagus season, April–June) is often explained in Chinese as 白芦笋季.

profile.feeling: Purple-flecked desserts, taro milk tea, Mid-Autumn home cooking.

senses.def: (dialectal Mandarin, e.g. Shandong, Anhui) sweet potato; (Henan, Yunnan) potato

examples.text: 芋头蒸熟以后又软又香。
examples.tr: Steamed taro is soft and fragrant.
examples.py: Yùtou zhēngshú yǐhòu yòu ruǎn yòu xiāng.

examples.text: 我想喝芋头奶茶。
examples.tr: I’d like a taro milk tea.
examples.py: Wǒ xiǎng hē yùtou nǎichá.

examples.text: 削芋头的时候要戴手套，不然手会痒。
examples.tr: Wear gloves when you peel taro, or your hands will itch.
examples.py: Xiāo yùtou de shíhou yào dài shǒutào, bùrán shǒu huì yǎng.

collocations.tr: ‘fragrant taro’ — taro flavour in sweets and drinks

synonyms.nuance: yù nǎi: the written word, and the everyday one around Shanghai
the single character: classical, written, and in compounds (芋泥, 芋圆)
the Sichuanese word

etymology.text: 芋: phono-semantic compound, 艸 ‘plant’ + phonetic 于 — taro. The ultimate origin is unclear: Shuowen links it to the taro’s startling size (probably folk etymology); compare Proto-Hmong-Mien *wouH ‘taro’ and Burmese ဝ (wa.) ‘elephant-foot yam’. 头 (‘head’, here a toneless noun suffix) is added as in 石头, 木头.

funFacts: In Cyprus taro is κολοκάσι — a name from the plant’s Latin genus Colocasia — and a traditional Cypriot dish.
Bright purple ‘taro’ desserts are often coloured: taro flesh itself is pale with purple flecks.
pitfalls: 头 is toneless here: yùtou, not yù tóu.
In some Mandarin dialects 芋头 means sweet potato or even potato (Wiktionary) — in standard Mandarin it is taro.
Raw taro irritates the skin and mouth; it must always be cooked.
subtleties: 毛芋头 ‘hairy taro’ are the small side corms; the big central corm is sold for taro paste and cakes.

profile.feeling: Crunchy slices with holes, Hubei soups, lotus ponds — and lingering love.

senses.def: lotus root (the rhizome of the lotus)

examples.text: 莲藕排骨汤是湖北的家常汤。
examples.tr: Lotus root and pork rib soup is a home-style soup from Hubei.
examples.py: Lián'ǒu páigǔ tāng shì Húběi de jiācháng tāng.

examples.text: 切开莲藕，里面有很多孔。
examples.tr: Cut open a lotus root and there are lots of holes inside.
examples.py: Qiēkāi lián'ǒu, lǐmiàn yǒu hěn duō kǒng.

examples.text: 我买两节莲藕。
examples.tr: I’ll buy two sections of lotus root.
examples.py: Wǒ mǎi liǎng jié lián'ǒu.

collocations.tr: lotus root and pork rib soup

phrases.tr: the lotus root breaks but its threads stay joined
phrases.meaning: a relationship is over but the feelings (or ties) linger

synonyms.nuance: the short word: in writing, in Beijing and the north-east, and in compounds (藕片, 藕粉)

etymology.text: 莲 (‘lotus’) + 藕 (‘lotus root’). 藕 is a phono-semantic compound: 艸 ‘grass, plant’ + phonetic 耦; it is attested late, earliest in the Erya.

funFacts: When you snap a lotus root, sticky threads stretch between the halves — hence the idiom 藕断丝连 for lovers who can’t quite let go.
莲 lián sounds like 怜 lián (‘to love, to pity’), so the lotus is a classic love symbol in old folk songs.
pitfalls: Pinyin needs the apostrophe: lián'ǒu — otherwise it could be read lián + ǒu or liá + nǒu.
藕 is ǒu (3rd tone).
subtleties: 荷 also means lotus: 荷花 is the lotus flower and 荷叶 the leaf; the root is 藕 or 莲藕.

profile.feeling: Childhood: blowing the seed heads; spring foraging; a herbal-tea word.

examples.text: 孩子们喜欢吹蒲公英。
examples.tr: Children love blowing dandelion clocks.
examples.py: Háizimen xǐhuan chuī púgōngyīng.

examples.text: 春天可以挖蒲公英做凉菜。
examples.tr: In spring you can dig up dandelions to make a cold dish.
examples.py: Chūntiān kěyǐ wā púgōngyīng zuò liángcài.

examples.text: 蒲公英泡水喝有点儿苦。
examples.tr: Dandelion steeped in hot water tastes a little bitter.
examples.py: Púgōngyīng pào shuǐ hē yǒudiǎnr kǔ.

synonyms.nuance: the folk name in Beijing and the north-east, used especially for the edible plant

etymology.text: 蒲 (‘cattail, rush’) + 公 (‘lord, old man’) + 英 (‘blossom’). Wiktionary gives no etymology; how the name arose is unclear.

funFacts: English dandelion comes from French dent de lion ‘lion’s tooth’, and German Löwenzahn says the same — both after the toothed leaves.
Russian одуванчик comes from дуть ‘to blow’ — the same game as Chinese 吹蒲公英.
pitfalls: 英 here is ‘blossom’, not ‘England, English’ (英国, 英语).
subtleties: As food it counts as a 野菜 (wild vegetable); in pharmacies it is a common herb of Chinese medicine.

profile.feeling: A bookish, botanical word; in the north people say 蔓菁.

examples.text: 芜菁和萝卜长得有点儿像。
examples.tr: Turnips look a bit like radishes.
examples.py: Wújīng hé luóbo zhǎng de yǒudiǎnr xiàng.

examples.text: 西方的炖菜里常放芜菁。
examples.tr: Western stews often contain turnip.
examples.py: Xīfāng de dùncài li cháng fàng wújīng.

examples.text: 很多北方人把芜菁叫蔓菁。
examples.tr: Many northerners call the turnip 蔓菁.
examples.py: Hěn duō běifāngrén bǎ wújīng jiào mánjing.

synonyms.nuance: mán jing: the traditional name, still the everyday word in much of the north and north-west (Shandong, Henan, Shaanxi, Shanxi, Ningxia, Qinghai)

etymology.text: 芜 (grass radical + 无) + 菁 (grass radical + 青 ‘green’); 菁 also appears in the synonym 蔓菁. The Classical Chinese word for the turnip was 葑 (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Book of Songs (诗经) line 采葑采菲 ‘picking turnips, picking radishes’ uses the old word 葑 for the turnip.
pitfalls: 大头菜 can mean turnip, kohlrabi, rutabaga or a pickled mustard root depending on the region — avoid it when you need to be precise.
芜 has the grass radical; 无 without it means ‘not have’.
subtleties: In everyday speech many people simply say 萝卜 for anything turnip-like; 芜菁 is the precise word.

profile.feeling: Bitter salad leaves, chicory coffee, imported Belgian endive.

examples.text: 菊苣有一点儿苦，适合做沙拉。
examples.tr: Chicory is slightly bitter and good in salads.
examples.py: Jújù yǒu yìdiǎnr kǔ, shìhé zuò shālā.

examples.text: 比利时菊苣是在黑暗里长出来的。
examples.tr: Belgian endive is grown in the dark.
examples.py: Bǐlìshí jújù shì zài hēi'àn li zhǎng chūlai de.

examples.text: 以前有人用菊苣根代替咖啡。
examples.tr: People used to use chicory root as a coffee substitute.
examples.py: Yǐqián yǒu rén yòng jújù gēn dàitì kāfēi.

profile.synonymsNone: 菊苣 is the only standard name; varieties are named by adding a word: 比利时菊苣 (Belgian endive), 红菊苣 (radicchio).

etymology.text: 菊 (‘chrysanthemum’; in compounds any plant of the daisy family) + 苣 (‘lettuce’): a ‘daisy-family lettuce’.

funFacts: English chicory and German Zichorie come, via Latin cichorium, from Greek κιχώριον.
Chicory-root coffee (German Zichorienkaffee) was a common coffee substitute in Germany in hard times.
pitfalls: English ‘endive’ and ‘chicory’ swap meanings between British and American usage; in Chinese 菊苣 is chicory/Belgian endive and 苦苣 is curly endive.
subtleties: 菊 in plant names marks the daisy family: 菊苣, 菊芋, 苦菊.

profile.feeling: A summer weed from the roadside that grandmothers turn into fillings and salads.

examples.text: 夏天路边常常长着马齿苋。
examples.tr: In summer purslane often grows by the roadside.
examples.py: Xiàtiān lùbiān chángcháng zhǎngzhe mǎchǐxiàn.

examples.text: 凉拌马齿苋酸酸的，很开胃。
examples.tr: Purslane salad is slightly sour and whets the appetite.
examples.py: Liángbàn mǎchǐxiàn suānsuān de, hěn kāiwèi.

examples.text: 我奶奶会用马齿苋包包子。
examples.tr: My grandma makes steamed buns filled with purslane.
examples.py: Wǒ nǎinai huì yòng mǎchǐxiàn bāo bāozi.

synonyms.nuance: ‘melon-seed greens’, after the small leaves
‘horse-tooth greens’

etymology.text: 马齿 (‘horse teeth’) + 苋 (‘amaranth’). The name is traditionally explained by its leaves, lined up like a horse’s teeth, and its amaranth-like texture.

funFacts: Purslane is γλιστρίδα in Greek and semizotu in Turkish — in both countries a classic summer salad with yogurt.
pitfalls: 齿 chǐ is 3rd tone: mǎ + chǐ follows tone sandhi in speech (máchǐxiàn), which is why Wiktionary lists both pronunciations.
subtleties: 苋菜 (amaranth greens) is a different vegetable; 马齿苋 is gathered as a 野菜 (wild green) and also sold in markets.

profile.feeling: Knobbly tubers, crunchy pickles; a yellow-flowered sunflower cousin.

examples.text: 菊芋常常做成咸菜，大家叫它洋姜。
examples.tr: Jerusalem artichokes are often pickled, and people call them 洋姜.
examples.py: Júyù chángcháng zuòchéng xiáncài, dàjiā jiào tā yángjiāng.

examples.text: 菊芋开黄花，有点儿像向日葵。
examples.tr: Jerusalem artichoke has yellow flowers, a bit like sunflowers.
examples.py: Júyù kāi huánghuā, yǒudiǎnr xiàng xiàngrìkuí.

examples.text: 菊芋的块茎可以生吃，也可以炒。
examples.tr: Jerusalem-artichoke tubers can be eaten raw or stir-fried.
examples.py: Júyù de kuàijīng kěyǐ shēng chī, yě kěyǐ chǎo.

synonyms.nuance: ‘foreign ginger’: the everyday name in most of northern and western China, especially for the pickled tuber
‘devil ginger’ — 鬼子 is an old derogatory word for foreigners

etymology.text: 菊 (‘daisy family’) + 芋 (‘taro, tuber’): a tuber from a daisy-family plant.

funFacts: Neither from Jerusalem nor an artichoke: the English name is often explained as a corruption of Italian girasole ‘sunflower’; German Topinambur is named after the Tupinambá people of Brazil.
pitfalls: 洋姜 is not ginger (姜) at all — the knobbly shape gave it the name.
subtleties: 菊芋 is the botanical and standard name; 洋姜 is what you hear at the market and on pickle jars.

profile.feeling: A stinging weed; in Europe a spring soup.

senses.def: nettle, stinging nettle (Urtica), incl. its young leaves as greens

examples.text: 碰到荨麻，皮肤会又痒又疼。
examples.tr: If you touch nettles, your skin itches and stings.
examples.py: Pèngdào qiánmá, pífū huì yòu yǎng yòu téng.

examples.text: 欧洲有人用嫩荨麻叶做汤。
examples.tr: In Europe some people make soup from young nettle leaves.
examples.py: Ōuzhōu yǒu rén yòng nèn qiánmá yè zuò tāng.

examples.text: 摘荨麻一定要戴手套。
examples.tr: Always wear gloves when picking nettles.
examples.py: Zhāi qiánmá yídìng yào dài shǒutào.

profile.synonymsNone: No other common name in Standard Mandarin; the reading xúnmá is used in Taiwan.

etymology.text: 荨 (grass radical + 寻) + 麻 (‘hemp; fibre plant’). Wiktionary records two readings, qiánmá and xúnmá.

funFacts: Greek τσουκνίδα (nettle) goes into spring pies, τσουκνιδόπιτα; Russian крапива into green soup.
Nettle fibre was once woven like linen; German Nesseltuch (‘nettle cloth’) still names a plain cotton fabric.
pitfalls: Mainland standard: 荨麻 is qiánmá, but in 荨麻疹 (hives) the same character is read xún: xúnmázhěn.
subtleties: Most Chinese speakers know the plant as a stinging weed and from the word 荨麻疹; eating nettles is more of a European habit.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; the name and pinyin come from the translations in the English entry “ramsons”.

profile.feeling: A European spring-forest green, smelling of garlic; known in China mainly from books and recipes.

senses.def: ramsons, wild garlic, bear’s garlic (Allium ursinum)

examples.text: 熊葱是欧洲春天的野菜。
examples.tr: Ramsons are a European spring wild green.
examples.py: Xióngcōng shì Ōuzhōu chūntiān de yěcài.

examples.text: 熊葱的叶子有很浓的大蒜味。
examples.tr: Wild-garlic leaves smell strongly of garlic.
examples.py: Xióngcōng de yèzi yǒu hěn nóng de dàsuàn wèi.

examples.text: 很多德国人春天去森林里采熊葱。
examples.tr: Many Germans go into the woods in spring to pick wild garlic.
examples.py: Hěn duō Déguórén chūntiān qù sēnlín li cǎi xióngcōng.

synonyms.nuance: ‘wild chives’: a loose everyday name for wild alliums in general, not specifically this species

etymology.text: 熊 (‘bear’) + 葱 (‘onion, scallion’): a calque of the species name Allium ursinum, ‘bear’s allium’ — the same image as German Bärlauch and English bear’s garlic.

funFacts: German Bärlauch, English bear’s garlic and Chinese 熊葱 all keep the bear of the Latin name.
pitfalls: Wild-garlic leaves look like those of poisonous lily of the valley (铃兰) and autumn crocus — foragers crush a leaf to check for the garlic smell.
subtleties: Rarely sold in China; the word is met mainly in translations, botany and European recipes.

profile.feeling: A pale, sweet European root; British Christmas dinners.

examples.text: 欧防风长得像白色的胡萝卜。
examples.tr: A parsnip looks like a white carrot.
examples.py: Ōufángfēng zhǎng de xiàng báisè de húluóbo.

examples.text: 烤欧防风有一点儿甜。
examples.tr: Roast parsnip is slightly sweet.
examples.py: Kǎo ōufángfēng yǒu yìdiǎnr tián.

examples.text: 英国人圣诞节常吃烤欧防风。
examples.tr: The British often eat roast parsnips at Christmas.
examples.py: Yīngguórén Shèngdànjié cháng chī kǎo ōufángfēng.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday Chinese name: the vegetable is little known in China, and 欧防风 is the dictionary and botanical name.

etymology.text: 欧 (‘Europe’, short for 欧洲) + 防风 (Saposhnikovia divaricata, a Chinese medicinal root, literally ‘ward off wind’): ‘the European 防风’, a relative in the carrot family.

funFacts: Russian пастернак means parsnip — so the poet Boris Pasternak’s surname is ‘Parsnip’; German says Pastinake.
pitfalls: 防风 alone is a Chinese medicinal herb, not the vegetable — keep the 欧.
subtleties: 欧 in plant names marks plants from Europe, as 洋 (‘overseas’) does in 洋葱, 洋姜.

profile.feeling: Lemony-sour leaves; French and Russian green soups.

examples.text: 酸模的叶子是酸的。
examples.tr: Sorrel leaves are sour.
examples.py: Suānmó de yèzi shì suān de.

examples.text: 法国菜里有一道酸模汤。
examples.tr: French cuisine has a sorrel soup.
examples.py: Fǎguó cài li yǒu yí dào suānmó tāng.

examples.text: 俄罗斯人夏天喝酸模做的绿汤。
examples.tr: In summer Russians eat a green soup made with sorrel.
examples.py: Éluósīrén xiàtiān hē suānmó zuò de lǜ tāng.

profile.synonymsNone: 酸模 is the only established name; sorrel is not a common market vegetable in China.

etymology.text: 酸 (‘sour’) + 模 (mó): the first part names the sour taste; Wiktionary gives no etymology for the word.

funFacts: Russian щавель goes into зелёные щи (green shchi), the summer ‘green borscht’.
pitfalls: 模 is read mó here (as in 模范), not mú (as in 模样).
subtleties: The sourness comes from oxalic acid (草酸), so sorrel is eaten in moderation.

profile.feeling: A sharp heat that shoots up the nose; sushi counters and Russian aspic.

examples.text: 吃生鱼片的时候，很多人蘸辣根。
examples.tr: When eating sashimi, many people dip it in horseradish paste.
examples.py: Chī shēngyúpiàn de shíhou, hěn duō rén zhàn làgēn.

examples.text: 辣根冲鼻子。
examples.tr: Horseradish goes right up your nose.
examples.py: Làgēn chōng bízi.

examples.text: 俄罗斯人吃肉冻的时候常配辣根。
examples.tr: Russians often have horseradish with meat aspic.
examples.py: Éluósīrén chī ròudòng de shíhou cháng pèi làgēn.

synonyms.nuance: properly ‘mustard’, but in everyday speech also the green paste served with sushi, which is usually horseradish-based

etymology.text: 辣 (‘hot, pungent’) + 根 (‘root’): the ‘hot root’.

funFacts: Most ‘wasabi’ outside Japan is horseradish coloured green; real wasabi is 山葵.
Austrian and Bavarian German Kren is a loan from Slavic — Russian хрен, the same root.
pitfalls: 辣根 (horseradish) is not 山葵 (wasabi), although tubes of paste are sold under both names.
subtleties: In Chinese restaurants the green paste is usually called 芥末, even though it is neither mustard nor wasabi.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; the name comes from the translations in the English entry “rutabaga”.

profile.feeling: A long botanical name for a humble yellow root from northern Europe.

examples.text: 芜菁甘蓝是芜菁和甘蓝杂交来的。
examples.tr: The rutabaga comes from a cross between turnip and cabbage.
examples.py: Wújīng gānlán shì wújīng hé gānlán zájiāo lái de.

examples.text: 芜菁甘蓝的肉是黄色的。
examples.tr: Rutabaga flesh is yellow.
examples.py: Wújīng gānlán de ròu shì huángsè de.

examples.text: 芜菁甘蓝可以煮汤，也可以做成泥。
examples.tr: Rutabaga can go into soup or be mashed.
examples.py: Wújīng gānlán kěyǐ zhǔ tāng, yě kěyǐ zuòchéng ní.

profile.synonymsNone: No common everyday name in China; 芜菁甘蓝 (‘turnip-cabbage’) is the dictionary and botanical name.

etymology.text: 芜菁 (‘turnip’) + 甘蓝 (‘cabbage, Brassica oleracea’): the name describes the plant as a turnip–cabbage hybrid, which it is.

funFacts: English ‘swede’ is short for ‘Swedish turnip’; in Germany the Steckrübe was the famine food of the ‘turnip winter’ (Steckrübenwinter) of 1916–17.
pitfalls: Not 芜菁 (turnip): a rutabaga is bigger, yellow-fleshed and has a purple top.
subtleties: Long descriptive names like this are typical for vegetables rarely grown in China.

profile.feeling: Cantonese slow-cooked soups; a Hong Kong street name.

examples.text: 广东人喜欢煲西洋菜汤。
examples.tr: Cantonese people like to slow-cook watercress soup.
examples.py: Guǎngdōngrén xǐhuan bāo xīyángcài tāng.

examples.text: 西洋菜长在水里，要洗干净。
examples.tr: Watercress grows in water, so wash it well.
examples.py: Xīyángcài zhǎng zài shuǐ li, yào xǐ gānjìng.

examples.text: 我买一把西洋菜。
examples.tr: I’ll buy a bunch of watercress.
examples.py: Wǒ mǎi yì bǎ xīyángcài.

synonyms.nuance: the standard written and botanical name
short Cantonese form

etymology.text: 西洋 (‘the West, Europe; overseas’) + 菜 (‘vegetable’): the ‘Western vegetable’.

funFacts: Sai Yeung Choi Street (西洋菜街) in Mong Kok, Hong Kong, is named after the watercress fields that once grew there.
pitfalls: 西洋 means ‘the West’; 西洋菜 is watercress, while Western food is 西餐.
subtleties: The name spread from Cantonese with Cantonese soups; 豆瓣菜 is what botanical works use.

profile.feeling: Summer, garlic stir-fries, southern and South-East Asian home cooking.

examples.text: 蒜蓉炒空心菜是很常见的家常菜。
examples.tr: Water spinach stir-fried with garlic is a very common home dish.
examples.py: Suànróng chǎo kōngxīncài shì hěn chángjiàn de jiāchángcài.

examples.text: 空心菜的茎是空的。
examples.tr: The stems of water spinach are hollow.
examples.py: Kōngxīncài de jīng shì kōng de.

examples.text: 夏天空心菜很便宜。
examples.tr: Water spinach is cheap in summer.
examples.py: Xiàtiān kōngxīncài hěn piányi.

synonyms.nuance: wèng cài: the standard written and botanical name; also the everyday word in Cantonese and in parts of the south-west
‘through-vegetable’, after the hollow stem
‘vine vegetable’

etymology.text: 空 (‘empty, hollow’) + 心 (‘heart, core’) + 菜 (‘vegetable’): its stems are hollow.

funFacts: In the Ming novel 封神演义 (Investiture of the Gods), the minister Bi Gan, whose heart has been cut out, meets a woman selling ‘heartless vegetable’ (无心菜); when she says a person without a heart cannot live, he dies.
Thai ‘morning glory’ stir-fry (pak bung) is the same vegetable.
pitfalls: 空 here is kōng (‘hollow’), not kòng (‘free time’).
subtleties: Wiktionary labels 空心菜 colloquial and 蕹菜 formal, but 空心菜 is what almost everyone says and what menus print.

profile.feeling: The crisp fried shallots on Taiwanese braised-pork rice.

examples.text: 红葱头切碎炸香，就是油葱酥。
examples.tr: Chop shallots and fry them crisp, and you have fried shallots (油葱酥).
examples.py: Hóngcōngtóu qiēsuì zhá xiāng, jiù shì yóucōngsū.

examples.text: 台湾的卤肉饭离不开红葱头。
examples.tr: Taiwanese braised-pork rice can’t do without shallots.
examples.py: Táiwān de lǔròufàn lí bu kāi hóngcōngtóu.

examples.text: 红葱头比洋葱小，味道更甜。
examples.tr: Shallots are smaller than onions and taste sweeter.
examples.py: Hóngcōngtóu bǐ yángcōng xiǎo, wèidào gèng tián.

synonyms.nuance: another common name for the same plant, used in parts of China

etymology.text: 红 (‘red’) + 葱 (‘onion, scallion’) + 头 (‘head, bulb’): the ‘red onion head’, after its reddish skin.

funFacts: English shallot and German Schalotte go back, via Latin, to the city of Ashkelon (Hebrew אַשְׁקְלוֹן) — the plant’s Latin name is Allium ascalonicum.
pitfalls: Not 紫洋葱 (red onion): shallots are smaller and grow in clusters of bulbs.
subtleties: 头 keeps its 2nd tone here (hóngcōngtóu), unlike the toneless 头 of 芋头 yùtou.

profile.feeling: Nourishing soups, slippery white flesh, Henan’s ‘iron-rod’ yams.

examples.text: 山药炖排骨很补。
examples.tr: Yam braised with pork ribs is very nourishing.
examples.py: Shānyao dùn páigǔ hěn bǔ.

examples.text: 削山药的时候手会痒。
examples.tr: Your hands itch when you peel yam.
examples.py: Xiāo shānyao de shíhou shǒu huì yǎng.

examples.text: 铁棍山药是河南的特产。
examples.tr: ‘Iron-rod’ yam is a speciality of Henan.
examples.py: Tiěgùn shānyao shì Hénán de tèchǎn.

collocations.tr: yam with blueberry sauce (a cold dish)

synonyms.nuance: shǔyù: the written and botanical name
the Cantonese word, especially for dried yam slices in soups and Chinese medicine

etymology.text: Named because it grows in the mountains (山) and is used as a medicine (药). A folk story says 山药 replaced the older 薯蓣 to avoid the personal names of Tang and Song emperors, but 山药 is already attested in the Jin dynasty (265–420).

funFacts: The taboo story is a good example of naming taboos (避讳): characters in an emperor’s name could not be used — but the dates show this one is folk etymology.
pitfalls: 药 is toneless in 山药: shānyao.
In American English ‘yam’ often means a sweet potato (红薯) — 山药 is a true yam, a different plant.
subtleties: In some northern dialects 山药 means sweet potato or potato (Wiktionary); standard Mandarin uses it for the Chinese yam.

profile.feeling: Sharp, slightly bitter greens; the source of China’s great pickles.

examples.text: 芥菜可以腌成咸菜。
examples.tr: Mustard greens can be pickled.
examples.py: Jiècài kěyǐ yānchéng xiáncài.

examples.text: 四川的榨菜是芥菜的一种。
examples.tr: Sichuan zhacai is a kind of mustard plant.

examples.text: 芥菜炒肉丝很好吃。
examples.tr: Mustard greens stir-fried with shredded pork are delicious.
examples.py: Jiècài chǎo ròusī hěn hǎochī.

synonyms.nuance: in South-western Mandarin 青菜 is leaf mustard; elsewhere it means ‘greens’ or bok choy
a written name given by Wiktionary for this vegetable

etymology.text: 芥 (‘mustard plant’) + 菜 (‘vegetable’).

funFacts: Sichuan 榨菜, the 雪里蕻 of Jiangnan and Cantonese-Hakka 梅菜 are all made from varieties of mustard.
English mustard comes from Latin mustum ‘grape must’, which was mixed with the ground seeds.
pitfalls: 芥 has two readings: jiè (芥末 ‘mustard’, 芥菜) and, colloquially, gài (芥菜 gàicài, 芥蓝 gàilán) — Wiktionary lists both.
subtleties: 芥蓝 (gai lan, ‘Chinese kale’) is a different vegetable despite sharing 芥.

profile.feeling: A Silk-Road name for a leafy beet; at the market more often ‘cowhide greens’.

senses.def: chard, Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris, leaf beet)

examples.text: 莙荙菜的叶柄有红的、黄的，也有白的。
examples.tr: Chard stalks can be red, yellow or white.
examples.py: Jūndácài de yèbǐng yǒu hóng de, huáng de, yě yǒu bái de.

examples.text: 莙荙菜和甜菜根是同一个物种。
examples.tr: Chard and beetroot are the same species.
examples.py: Jūndácài hé tiáncàigēn shì tóng yí ge wùzhǒng.

examples.text: 四川人把莙荙菜叫牛皮菜。
examples.tr: Sichuanese call chard 牛皮菜.
examples.py: Sìchuānrén bǎ jūndácài jiào niúpícài.

synonyms.nuance: ‘cowhide greens’, after the thick leaves; the usual market name in the south-west
‘leaf beet’, the descriptive written name
‘thick-skin greens’

etymology.text: An old loanword: 莙薘 is attested since the 5th century. The 8th-century Jingxingji says the vegetable came from 末禄 (perhaps Merv in Turkmenistan). It is an Iranian loan matching Middle Persian *gundar; compare Persian چغندر (čoġondar) ‘beet’.

funFacts: The Chinese name is Persian: 莙薘 jūndá matches Middle Persian *gundar, and Persian still says چغندر (čoġondar) for beet — a Silk Road loanword.
pitfalls: Don’t confuse with 甜菜 (sugar beet) or 甜菜根 (beetroot): chard is eaten for its leaves.
Traditional 莙薘菜 has 達 under the grass radical; the simplified form is 莙荙菜.
subtleties: The name varies a lot by region; 莙荙菜 is the dictionary word, many markets say 牛皮菜.

profile.feeling: Spring in the south: fresh shoots, crunchy and sweet; pandas.

examples.text: 春天的竹笋特别鲜。
examples.tr: Bamboo shoots in spring are especially fresh and tasty.
examples.py: Chūntiān de zhúsǔn tèbié xiān.

examples.text: 雨后的竹笋长得很快。
examples.tr: After rain, bamboo shoots grow very fast.
examples.py: Yǔ hòu de zhúsǔn zhǎng de hěn kuài.

phrases.tr: like bamboo shoots after spring rain
phrases.meaning: springing up quickly and in great numbers

synonyms.nuance: the short everyday form, very common in compounds (春笋, 笋干)
with the noun suffix 子

etymology.text: 竹 (‘bamboo’) + 笋 (‘shoot’). Traditional 筍 is a phono-semantic compound: 竹 ‘bamboo’ + phonetic 旬.

funFacts: In Cantonese slang 筍 means a bargain, something good value (Wiktionary).
Some bamboos grow almost a metre a day; the idiom 雨后春笋 captures that speed.
pitfalls: Simplified 笋 has 尹 under the bamboo radical; traditional 筍 has 旬.
笋 alone means the bamboo shoot, but 芦笋 is asparagus — a different plant.
subtleties: 冬笋 (winter shoots, dug up before they break the surface) are prized and dearer than 春笋.

profile.feeling: Peppery leaves on pizza and Western salads.

examples.tr: A handful of arugula was put on the pizza.

examples.tr: Italians often use arugula in salads.
examples.py: Yìdàlìrén zuò shālā cháng yòng zhīmacài.

profile.synonymsNone: 芝麻菜 is the only established Mandarin name (Wiktionary lists no other).

etymology.text: 芝麻 (‘sesame’) + 菜 (‘vegetable’): named after its nutty, sesame-like taste.

funFacts: Italian rucola, German Rucola/Rauke, Greek ρόκα, Turkish roka and English rocket all go back to Latin eruca.
pitfalls: 麻 is toneless in 芝麻: zhīmacài.
芝麻菜 is not sesame leaves (芝麻叶).
subtleties: The leaves get hotter and more peppery as the plant grows older.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; the name comes from the translations in the English entry “corn salad”.

profile.feeling: A small European winter salad, almost unknown in Chinese markets.

examples.text: 野苣的叶子小小的、圆圆的。
examples.tr: Lamb’s lettuce has small, round leaves.
examples.py: Yějù de yèzi xiǎoxiǎo de, yuányuán de.

synonyms.nuance: ‘lettuce valerian’, a botanical name: the plant is a relative of valerian

etymology.text: 野 (‘wild’) + 苣 (‘lettuce’): ‘wild lettuce’.

funFacts: In parts of Germany Feldsalat is called Rapunzel — the fairy-tale girl is named after the salad her mother craved from the witch’s garden.
pitfalls: A translation name: many Chinese speakers won’t know it; 野菜 (‘wild vegetables’) is a different, general word.
subtleties: 苣 turns up in lettuce-type names: 莴苣, 菊苣, 苦苣, 野苣.

profile.feeling: Dumplings and chive pockets; strong breath; online, the fleeced small investor.

examples.text: 我最喜欢吃韭菜鸡蛋饺子。

the Cantonese and Hakka word

etymology.text: 韭 (‘chive’) + 菜 (‘vegetable’). The slang sense comes from the fact that garlic chives grow back after they are cut (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Chives grow back after cutting — hence 割韭菜 ‘harvesting the chives’ for exploiting the same small investors over and over (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: 韭菜 (garlic chives) ≠ 韭葱 (leek) ≠ 葱 (spring onion).
韭 jiǔ is 3rd tone.
subtleties: 韭黄 (blanched chives) are grown in the dark; 韭菜花 (chive flowers) are eaten too, and a chive-flower sauce goes with Beijing lamb hotpot.

profile.feeling: Winter soups and braises; a plain, healthy, everyday root.

pitfalls: 卜 is toneless: báiluóbo.
subtleties: 胡萝卜 (carrot) is the ‘foreign radish’; 白 is what marks the native white one.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; checked against 生菜 (‘romaine lettuce; lettuce’) and 罗马 (‘Rome’).

profile.feeling: Caesar salad, supermarket salad bags; crisp and long-leaved.

examples.text: 凯撒沙拉要用罗马生菜。
examples.tr: Caesar salad needs romaine lettuce.

etymology.text: 罗马 (‘Rome’) + 生菜 (‘lettuce’): ‘Roman lettuce’, a translation of French laitue romaine.

funFacts: English ‘cos’ is traditionally traced to the Greek island of Kos; in Greece this long-leaved type is the everyday μαρούλι.
pitfalls: 油麦菜 (a long-leaved Chinese lettuce eaten cooked) looks similar but is a different variety.
subtleties: Wiktionary’s first meaning of plain 生菜 is ‘romaine lettuce’; in shops 罗马生菜 makes the variety explicit.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; checked against 菊苣 (‘chicory’).

profile.feeling: A wine-red, bitter Italian leaf in imported salad mixes.

examples.text: 红菊苣的叶子是紫红色的，有白色的叶脉。
examples.tr: Radicchio leaves are purplish red with white veins.
examples.py: Hóngjújù de yèzi shì zǐhóngsè de, yǒu báisè de yèmài.

examples.tr: Radicchio is a little bitter and goes well with sweet fruit.
examples.py: Hóngjújù yǒudiǎnr kǔ, shìhé pèi tián de shuǐguǒ.

etymology.text: 红 (‘red’) + 菊苣 (‘chicory’): ‘red chicory’, like Italian radicchio rosso.

funFacts: Radicchio di Treviso and di Chioggia are named after the Italian towns that grow them.
pitfalls: Don’t call it 紫甘蓝 (red cabbage): it looks similar but is a chicory — bitter and tender.
subtleties: An imported, restaurant vegetable in China; many people meet it only in salad mixes.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; it is a transparent compound, checked against 洋葱 (‘onion’; classifiers 颗, 个).

profile.feeling: Purple rings in cold dishes and salads; milder than the yellow onion.

examples.text: 紫洋葱比黄洋葱甜，适合生吃。

examples.text: 凉拌木耳里放了一点儿紫洋葱。

synonyms.nuance: equally common: the skin is called red or purple
‘purple-skinned onion’, the fuller market name

etymology.text: 紫 (‘purple’) + 洋葱 (‘onion’: 洋 ‘overseas’ + 葱 ‘scallion’).

funFacts: Turkish also sees it as purple: mor soğan ‘purple onion’, just like Chinese 紫洋葱, while English and German call it red.
pitfalls: 紫洋葱 (red onion) vs 紫甘蓝 (red cabbage) — the same 紫, different vegetables.
subtleties: A descriptive compound rather than a dictionary word: Wiktionary has no page for it, and 红洋葱 is just as normal.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; checked against 生菜 (‘lettuce’) and 西生菜 (‘iceberg lettuce’).

profile.feeling: Burgers and fast food; crunchy, watery, mild.

examples.text: 汉堡里的生菜一般是球生菜。
examples.tr: The lettuce in burgers is usually iceberg.
examples.py: Hànbǎo li de shēngcài yìbān shì qiú shēngcài.

examples.text: 球生菜很脆，水分很多。
examples.tr: Iceberg lettuce is crunchy and watery.
examples.py: Qiú shēngcài hěn cuì, shuǐfèn hěn duō.

examples.text: 我买一个球生菜。
examples.tr: I’ll buy a head of iceberg lettuce.
examples.py: Wǒ mǎi yí ge qiú shēngcài.

synonyms.nuance: ‘Western lettuce’; Wiktionary glosses it ‘iceberg lettuce’
‘rolled-heart lettuce’, a dictionary-style name

etymology.text: 球 (‘ball’) + 生菜 (‘lettuce’): ‘ball lettuce’, for its tight round head.

funFacts: The English name ‘iceberg’ comes from the heads being shipped across the US packed in ice.
pitfalls: Not 卷心菜 (cabbage), although both form round heads.
subtleties: In Chinese cooking iceberg is also blanched or stir-fried, e.g. with oyster sauce, not only eaten raw.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no Chinese entry for this word; the name comes from the translations in the English entry “endive” (Cichorium endivia).

profile.feeling: Curly, bitter leaves in cold dishes; at the market usually 苦菊.

examples.text: 苦苣的叶子卷卷的，有点儿苦。
examples.tr: Endive leaves are curly and a little bitter.
examples.py: Kǔjù de yèzi juǎnjuǎn de, yǒudiǎnr kǔ.

examples.text: 很多人把苦苣叫苦菊，常常凉拌着吃。
examples.tr: Many people call endive 苦菊 and often eat it as a cold dish.
examples.py: Hěn duō rén bǎ kǔjù jiào kǔjú, chángcháng liángbànzhe chī.

examples.text: 苦苣蘸酱吃很爽口。
examples.tr: Endive dipped in sauce is crisp and refreshing.
examples.py: Kǔjù zhàn jiàng chī hěn shuǎngkǒu.

synonyms.nuance: ‘bitter chrysanthemum’: the usual market and menu name on the Mainland (凉拌苦菊)

etymology.text: 苦 (‘bitter’) + 苣 (‘lettuce’): ‘bitter lettuce’.

funFacts: English endive goes back through Latin to Greek, and Greek still calls the plant αντίδι.
pitfalls: 苦苣菜 (sow thistle, Sonchus) is a different, wild plant despite the similar name.
subtleties: Curly frisée and broad-leaved escarole are both Cichorium endivia.

absent.reason: Garden cress (Lepidium sativum) has no common Chinese name; it is hardly grown or sold in China, and Wiktionary gives no Chinese word for it.
absent.use: Botanically it belongs to 独行菜属 (dúxíngcài shǔ, the pepperweed genus Lepidium); in shops cress sprouts are simply 芽苗菜 (sprout greens) or are described.

absent.reason: Black salsify (Scorzonera hispanica) is practically unknown as a vegetable in China; Wiktionary has no Chinese name for it.
absent.use: Botanical texts use names built on 鸦葱 (yācōng, the Scorzonera genus); in speech it is described, e.g. 一种黑皮的根菜 ‘a black-skinned root vegetable’.

absent.reason: Jute mallow is not a traditional Chinese vegetable and has no established everyday name; Wiktionary gives none.
absent.use: The plant is a jute: 黄麻 (huángmá) is jute in general, Corchorus olitorius is 长蒴黄麻 in botany; as a health vegetable it is sold in places as 帝王菜 (‘emperor’s greens’, echoing the Arabic name).

absent.reason: Celeriac is rare in Chinese markets and has no single established name; Wiktionary gives no Chinese word.
absent.use: Descriptive names such as 根芹 or 根芹菜 (‘root celery’) and 块根芹 are used in recipes and seed catalogues.
